hero.subtitle: The protocol behind Let's Encrypt that automated certificate issuance and renewal, bringing free HTTPS to the entire web.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
ACME (Automatic Certificate Management Environment) automates the process of verification and issuance of X.509 certificates. It was designed for Let's Encrypt but is used by many CAs.

Before ACME, getting an SSL certificate required manual steps, payment, and waiting. ACME made free, automated certificates possible, driving HTTPS adoption from ~40% to over 95% of web traffic.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
ACME is a JSON-based protocol over HTTPS. All requests are signed with the account's private key using JWS (JSON Web Signature).

Account CreationClient registers a public key with the CA server
OrderClient requests a certificate for one or more domain names
AuthorizationCA presents challenges to prove domain control
FinalizeClient submits CSR, CA issues the certificate

sections.title: Challenge Types
sections.content:
ACME supports multiple challenge types to prove domain control:

Challenge
Mechanism
HTTP-01
Place a file at /.well-known/acme-challenge/ on port 80
DNS-01
Create a TXT record _acme-challenge.domain
TLS-ALPN-01
Present a self-signed cert during TLS on port 443

DNS-01 is the only challenge type that supports wildcard certificates (*.example.com).

sections.title: Automated Renewal
sections.content:
ACME certificates are typically valid for 90 days, encouraging automation. Clients like Certbot, acme.sh, and Caddy handle automatic renewal.

Certbot
The most popular ACME client, developed by EFF. Supports Apache, Nginx, and standalone modes.
Short-Lived Certs
90-day validity reduces exposure if a key is compromised and encourages automation.
Rate Limits
Let's Encrypt enforces rate limits (50 certs per domain per week) to prevent abuse.
